title: Evaluate Nested Arithmetic
statement:
The string s is an arithmetic expression built from non-negative integers, the operators +, -, *, /, and parentheses ( ). It has no spaces. Return its value as an integer.

Use the usual rules: parentheses first, then * and /, then + and -. Operators of the same level apply from left to right. Integer division truncates toward zero, so -7 / 2 is -3, not -4.

The expression is always valid. There is no unary minus (-3 or (-2) never appear on their own), no division by zero, and every intermediate value fits in a 32-bit signed integer. Do not use eval or a similar built-in.

examples.why: The bracket gives 5, the multiplication gives 10, then 7 − 10.
14 / −5 is −2.8. Truncating toward zero gives −2; floor division would give −3.
Subtraction runs left to right: (10 − 2) − 3. A right-recursive parser that does 10 − (2 − 3) returns 11.

constraints: Every intermediate value fits in a 32-bit signed integer
hints: Without parentheses, a single stack of signed terms handles precedence: push numbers after + or −, and combine with the top after * or /.
A pair of parentheses is just a smaller expression of the same kind. When you see '(', you need to put the current work aside and start fresh.

Either recurse (a parser with expr → term → factor, where a factor may be a bracketed expr) or keep a stack of saved (terms, pending operator) frames: push one at '(' and pop it at ')', where the bracket's sum becomes the next number.

explain.intuition:
Inside one pair of parentheses the problem is the flat calculator: keep a list of signed terms, push a number after + or −, and fold it into the last term after * or /. The sum of the list is the value.

A bracket just interrupts that work. On (, save the current list and the operator waiting in front of the bracket, and start an empty list. On ), sum the inner list: that sum behaves exactly like a number that was written in the bracket's place, so restore the saved list and operator and carry on. It is the same as resolving a nested component tree: finish the child, hand back one value, continue in the parent. A recursive descent parser does the same thing, with the call stack doing the saving.
steps: Keep num = 0, op = '+', a list terms, and a stack frames.
On an operator, apply the pending op with num to terms (push, push negated, multiply the top, or divide the top truncating toward zero), then set op to this operator and num = 0.
On (, push [terms, op] to frames, then reset terms = [], op = '+'.
On ), apply the pending op, set num to the sum of terms, and pop [terms, op] back from frames.
At the end apply the pending op once more and return the sum of terms.
pitfalls: Floor division. Python's // and Math.floor round −2.8 down to −3; the rules want truncation toward zero.
Writing the grammar right-recursively (expr = term '-' expr), which makes 10-2-3 come out as 11.
Forgetting to restore the operator that stood before the bracket, so 2*(3+4) adds 7 instead of multiplying by it.

complexity.space: O(depth + n) for the saved frames and terms

solutions.title: Recursive descent parser
solutions.idea: Three small functions, one per precedence level: expr handles + and −, term handles * and /, factor reads a number or a bracketed expr. A shared index walks the string once.

solutions.title: Term stack with saved frames
solutions.idea: The flat calculator's stack of signed terms, plus a stack of frames: '(' saves the terms and the pending operator, ')' turns the inner sum into the next number.

followups: Add unary minus, so that -(2+3) and 4*-2 are valid. Where does each solution need to change?
Add variables: the expression may contain names, and you get a map from name to value. How would you also simplify an expression whose variables are unknown?
